title: Hanson v. Denckla (1958)
summary: A settlor’s later move to Florida did not create personal jurisdiction there over the Delaware trustee.
notes:
Distinguish the person whose conduct supplies the contact from the person who suffers the consequences. Also distinguish personal jurisdiction, property jurisdiction, and the authority to select governing law.

Verbatim rule: 'it is essential in each case that there be some act by which the defendant purposefully avails itself of the privilege of conducting activities within the forum State, thus invoking the benefits and protections of its laws'; the unilateral activity of those claiming a relationship with the defendant cannot supply the contact.

Dora Donner, a Pennsylvanian, created the trust with a Delaware trustee (Wilmington Trust Co.) and later moved to Florida, where she exercised the power of appointment and died; the Court (Warren, C.J., 5–4) held Florida lacked both in rem and in personam jurisdiction, reversed the Florida Supreme Court, and affirmed the Delaware Supreme Court's refusal to give the Florida decree full faith and credit; Justice Black's dissent was joined by Justices Burton and Brennan, and Justice Douglas dissented separately.

sections.Parties: The controversy involved competing beneficiaries of a trust established by Donner and the Delaware trustee holding its assets. Florida and Delaware proceedings addressed the effectiveness of arrangements affecting the trust property.
sections.Material Facts: Donner established the trust while connected to Pennsylvania and used a Delaware trustee. She subsequently moved to Florida. The trustee had no Florida office, did not solicit business there, and did not perform the relevant acts there merely because the settlor later resided there. The settlor’s Florida activities and the estate’s Florida connection gave that state an interest in the controversy, but they did not show that the trustee had chosen to engage in Florida activity.
sections.Procedural History: Proceedings in Florida and Delaware produced a dispute over the effectiveness and recognition of the trust-related adjudications. The Supreme Court concluded that Florida lacked the required jurisdiction over the trustee, whose participation was necessary to the attempted resolution. The Florida judgment could not bind the trustee in the manner asserted.
sections.Issue: Did the settlor’s residence and activities in Florida supply the minimum contacts needed to bind the out-of-state trustee?
sections.Holding: No. The necessary connection had to come from acts by which the defendant purposefully availed itself of conducting activities in the forum.
sections.Reasoning: The Court maintained a territorial limit on adjudicatory authority even while recognizing easier interstate travel and communication. A plaintiff or beneficiary cannot create the defendant’s forum affiliation by unilateral acts. The trustee’s relationship with Donner predated her move and was centered elsewhere. The forum’s interest, the convenience of resolving an estate in one place, and the possible relevance of Florida law could not supply the missing defendant-created contact. McGee involved the insurer’s own solicitation of a California relationship; that feature was absent here.

learning.why: A settlor’s later move to Florida did not create personal jurisdiction there over the Delaware trustee.

topics.purposeful-availment: The settlor’s move to Florida did not substitute for purposeful forum conduct by the Delaware trustee.
topics.relatedness: Florida’s connection to estate administration did not establish the trustee’s required forum connection.
topics.cp-required-joinder: The trustee’s absence mattered to the attempted adjudication of the trust.
topics.cp-choice-law: A state’s interest in applicable law or estate administration does not itself establish personal jurisdiction.
topics.minimum-contacts: Hanson supplies the purposeful-availment gloss on International Shoe's minimum-contacts test.
topics.cp-property-jurisdiction: The Court also held Florida lacked in rem jurisdiction because the trust assets were in Delaware.

learning.separateOpinions: Justice Black’s dissent emphasized Florida’s substantial connection to the settlor and controversy, and the practical fairness of resolving the connected estate issues there.

mnemonic.rationale: A Delaware trust and a Florida move
